activities.anchor: film shows 24 of them every second
activities.caption: guess the frame rate before it lands
activities.name: anFpsEstimate

config.prompt: How many still frames does film show every second?
config.why: 24 frames per second. Nothing in the notebook ever moved — yet the eye invented the motion across the gaps. That gap is the whole art form.
config.context: 24 stills a second, and your eye fills in every interval between them.

activities.anchor:
Half the list
    stylises real mechanics
activities.caption: file the twelve into their two parentages
activities.name: anFamilyBuckets

config.prompt: The twelve principles have a double parentage — physics and psychology fused. File each:
config.why: Half the list stylises inertia, arcs and momentum until they read at speed; the other half controls attention and feeling. That double parentage is why the list survived the jump from pencils to pixels unchanged.

activities.anchor: keeping its apparent volume
activities.caption: pair each principle with the problem it solves
activities.name: anProblemMatch

config.prompt: Each principle answers a specific problem. Match them:

pairs.right: how does a flat, weightless drawing seem to have mass
how does the eye parse an action that is over in eight frames
what decides whether motion reads as heavy, nervous or stately
what happens after the main pose has already ended

config.why: The rule that total volume stays constant is what keeps the deformation physical rather than a rubbery accident: if the ball flattens, it must also widen.

activities.anchor: the rule called slow in and slow out
activities.caption: which spacing chart falls like a real ball?
activities.name: anSpacingTrace

config.prompt: A ball bouncing once, drawn as position against time. Which curve is spaced the way gravity demands — bunched at the peak, stretched through the fall, landing hard?

curves.label: a straight line — evenly spaced drawings
a curve lingering at the top and accelerating into contact

config.why: Where the drawings cluster, the motion lingers; where they starve, it races. The straight line is the spreadsheet fall. In computer animation the same idea arrives as the easing curve — literally a spacing chart.

activities.anchor: the famous "smear" frame
activities.caption: true or false — what squash and stretch is really for
activities.name: anSquashJudge

statements.s: Squash and stretch is cartoon exaggeration, optional outside comedy.
statements.why: It is load-bearing in realistic work too, at subtler amplitude. Turning it off is one of the fastest ways to make expensive animation look like a puppet show.

statements.s: The eye reads the flexing as the effect of forces — the squash is the impact, the stretch the acceleration.
statements.why: That is why constant-volume deformation reads as weight rather than as rubber.

statements.s: If the ball flattens, it must also widen.
statements.why: Apparent volume stays constant — that is the rule that keeps the effect physical.

statements.s: A single distorted smear frame reads to an audience as breakage.
statements.why: The eye accepts constant-volume deformation as natural, so a smear bridges impossibly fast action and reads as speed and impact.

activities.anchor: a wind-up — a one- or two-frame dip
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this anticipation rule
activities.name: anAnticipationSpot

config.prompt: A student writes up the anticipation rule of thumb. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Anticipation moves the audience backwards before forwards: the crouch before the jump, the wind-up before the punch.
It sells the action physically and it tells the eye where to look and when.
Because anticipation costs frames, fast actions should skip it to keep their speed.
An action of ten frames or fewer is over in under half a second, so the eye needs a wind-up to parse it.
The rule of thumb is proportional: bigger action, bigger wind-up.
config.correction: The working rule is the opposite: the FASTER the action, the more it needs a wind-up.
config.why: Below about ten frames the eye cannot parse an action it did not see coming. Anticipation does not spend the audience's patience — it spends frames to buy legibility.

activities.anchor: successive breaking of joints
activities.caption: decide between simultaneity and cascade
activities.name: anOverlapBranch

config.root: You are animating a character turning and walking off. Every limb arrives on the same frame, each starting and stopping together.

start.text: The pose is correct. The timing of the parts is not.

choices.label: Keep it — simultaneous arrival looks crisp and controlled
choices.feedback: The same walk with every limb arriving on the same frame reads as marionette.

choices.label: Delay each joint slightly — arm after shoulder, fingers after arm
choices.feedback: Successive breaking of joints replaces a robot's simultaneity with the cascade real bodies perform.

simultaneous.text: Everything lands together and the character reads as a puppet — precise, weightless, dead on its feet.

cascade.text: The parts overrun and trail; the walk with dragging weight feels alive. And on a held pose, keep micro-drifting: a dead stop reads as death.

config.why: Nothing stops at once. Loosely attached parts overrun (follow-through), and no two parts move on exactly the same clock (overlapping action). The moving hold is the principle's modern descendant.

activities.anchor: straightening the arc makes
activities.caption: locate the frame budget for a punch
activities.name: anFastActionPlace

config.prompt: A thrown punch lasts eight frames. Place the marker at the frame count below which the eye cannot parse an action it did not see coming.
config.why: About ten frames. Below that the animator must add a wind-up — a one- or two-frame dip — to tell the eye where and when to look.

activities.anchor: passed on by teaching and imitation rather than genes
activities.caption: fill the three words that carry the theory
activities.name: anCultureCloze

config.text: Culture is the learned, shared and symbolic system through which a group makes a life. It is %%0%% — nobody is born knowing that forks go on the left, which means it can be reinstalled. It is %%1%% — it lives between people, in common expectations. And it is symbolic: a flag is cloth until meaning makes it otherwise.
config.hint: Both blanks are single adjectives from the definition's opening sentence.

activities.anchor: shape makes the point brutally
activities.caption: guess how compressed the last act is
activities.name: anTimelineEstimate

config.prompt: On a 300,000-year timeline, roughly what percentage of it passes before farming, cities, writing and industry arrive?
config.why: Roughly 285,000 years of foraging pass before everything we call civilisation is compressed into the final 5 percent. That acceleration is cultural inheritance compounding — genes needed a hundred thousand years to spread a trait.
config.context: The last five percent of the timeline holds everything after the savannah.

activities.anchor: islanders risk their
activities.caption: pair each celebrated practice with its internal logic
activities.name: anMeaningMatch

config.prompt: Practices that look irrational from outside usually do invisible work. Match each to what it accomplishes in its own terms:

pairs.right: circulating objects builds alliances, reputation and obligation across a sea of islands
status is earned by generosity, and the bank is obligation owed
a coherent system for explaining misfortune and sanctioning malice

pairs.left: eating or not eating a cow
pairs.right: a symbol cannot be translated one-for-one between economies

config.why: The rule that falls out: before asking whether a practice is efficient, ask what it accomplishes in its own terms. As trade the Kula looks absurd; as politics it is perfectly rational.

activities.anchor: Bronislaw Malinowski, stranded in the Trobriands
activities.caption: rebuild the method in order
activities.name: anMethodOrder

config.prompt: How anthropology knows what it knows — from immersion to a science of variation:
items: Immerse long-term in a community and learn the language
Participate in daily life and watch what people do, not only what they say
Write the disciplined account as ethnography, with reflexivity about the researcher's own position
Compare across cultures and across time to separate the local from the constant
config.why: One case is an anecdote; the discipline compares. That comparison is what separates anthropology from travel writing — it turns exotic particularity into a science of variation.

activities.anchor: the claim that no standard can judge anything
activities.caption: true or false — relativism as method versus philosophy
activities.name: anRelativismJudge

statements.s: Cultural relativism is the methodological rule to understand a practice in its own context first.
statements.why: It exists because judgements made instantly in your own categories are usually misreadings — it buys understanding and costs the comfort of instant verdicts.

statements.s: The discipline accepted the strong claim that no standard can judge anything.
statements.why: It never did. Anthropologists document infanticide, famine mismanagement and genocide as rigorously as gift exchange.

statements.s: Ethnocentrism is easy to catch because it announces itself.
statements.why: Catching it is harder than it sounds, because from inside, the ruler feels invisible.

statements.s: Judgement, if it follows, follows understanding.
statements.why: Relativism first, judgement later — and only after you can state the practice's logic so well its adherents would recognise it.

activities.anchor: the Scottish clan tartans were codified
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this picture of culture
activities.name: anProcessSpot

config.prompt: A student describes how culture moves through time. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Process insists that culture is always being made — a verb, not a noun.
Traditions that look ancient are regularly younger than they claim; the 19th-century tartans are one case.
Social reproduction means cultures are static museum pieces, preserved intact across generations.
Reproduction works through everyday transmission: what schools reward, what families model, what counts as acting properly.
Reproduction explains stubbornness; process explains change.
config.correction: Social reproduction means societies reproduce their arrangements across generations — not that cultures are static. Process explains change alongside it.
config.why: Bourdieu's habitus — the embodied dispositions that make social positions feel natural — is why inequality outlives the laws that produced it, without anyone legislating it.

activities.anchor: because in those systems the men
activities.caption: bet on the kinship insight
activities.name: anKinshipPredict

config.q: Many societies use one kinship term where English distinguishes 'father' from 'uncle'. What does that tell you?
choices: Their languages are simply less precise than English
Kinship is classificatory — a symbolic system in which those men are socially equivalent
They have no concept of individual parentage
The distinction exists but is considered impolite to name
config.why: Kinship assigns obligations before any state does: who feeds you, who avenges you, whom you may not marry. It is society's first grammar, written before writing.

activities.anchor: The small two-parent household is one local solution
activities.caption: file each claim about the family
activities.name: anFamilyBuckets

config.prompt: Is this a finding from the ethnographic record, or the misconception the lesson corrects? File each:

items.label: extended households are common and stable
matrilineal inheritance is a working answer
polygynous marriage is common and stable
the nuclear family is the natural, universal building block
other arrangements are deviations from the norm

config.why: The small two-parent household is one local solution — historically the minority variant — and its 'naturalness' is the thing that needs arguing, not assuming.

activities.anchor: Its unique asset is time depth
activities.caption: pair each field with its flagship
activities.name: anFieldsMatch

config.prompt: The four fields bracket the species — bones at one end, conversation at the other. Match each to its flagship:

pairs.right: the great comparative discoveries — gift economies, kinship systems, everyday rationality
time depth: the 10,000-year record of sedentism, agriculture, cities and statehood
the fossil record, primate relatives as controls, and skeletons that record diet and violence
how speech does social work — honorifics, kin terms, ritual speech that makes law

config.why: Together the four fields bracket the species. Archaeology's unique asset is the time depth no informant can supply.

activities.anchor:
the last few million
  years of stone tools
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this discipline map
activities.name: anArchaeologySpot

config.prompt: A student describes the four fields. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Cultural anthropology studies living societies through immersion and writes the result as ethnography.
Archaeology studies past societies through what they left in the ground: potsherds, house plans, middens, burials.
Archaeology's subject is dinosaurs and other fossils, which is why it shares a toolkit with palaeontology.
Biological anthropology studies humans as evolved organisms, including the hominin fossil record.
Linguistic anthropology studies language as cultural practice rather than grammar for its own sake.
config.correction: Dinosaur bones belong to palaeontology. Archaeology's subject is humans and their ancestors — the last few million years of stone tools, settlements, middens and burials.
config.why: When archaeologists do encounter animal bone, it is usually as food refuse or a worked artefact — evidence about people, not about the animals' own evolution.

activities.anchor: is invisible to a camera and decisive socially
activities.caption: decide what is and is not cultural data
activities.name: anWinkBranch

config.root: You film a person's eye closing. On the footage, a twitch and a wink look identical.

start.text: What does the discipline's unit of analysis require you to record?

choices.label: The behaviour — the eyelid moved, and that is the data
choices.feedback: A camera sees the same movement either way. That is the point of the example.

choices.label: The meaning — which act it was, and for whom
choices.feedback: The same physical act is a different act under different meanings.

behaviour.text: You have recorded a movement and missed the act. This is why the field documents categories before counting them.

meaning.text: Culture is that decisive layer — invisible to a camera, and thick description is the craft of writing it down.

config.why: The discipline's unit of analysis is not behaviour but meaningful behaviour. That is also why reflexivity matters: the analyst's own categories and assumptions are themselves cultural data.

activities.anchor: webs of significance
activities.caption: fill Geertz's working view
activities.name: anGeertzCloze

config.text: Tylor's 1871 definition still anchors textbooks. Geertz's refinement is the modern working view: culture as %%0%% of significance that humans spin and then suspend themselves in, readable by %%1%% description — the recording not just of an act but of its layered meaning.
config.hint: The metaphor names the image Geertz uses for the spun system; the description is the one named after its depth.

activities.anchor: the ethnographic present ("the Nuer do X")
activities.caption: true or false — process and the museum picture
activities.name: anProcessJudge

statements.s: Cultures are museum specimens whose arrangements persist automatically.
statements.why: Reproduction is never automatic — that is why every society spends so much effort on it.

statements.s: The ethnographic present is a writing convention, not a fact about time.
statements.why: Every tradition is being made, defended, borrowed and reinvented.

statements.s: Hobsbawm showed Highland kilts and colonial ceremonies being manufactured surprisingly late.
statements.why: The 'invention of tradition' — the kilts demonstrate that what looks ancient can be recent.

statements.s: Culture is holistic: religion, economy, kinship and ecology interlock.
statements.why: You cannot edit one strand without moving the others — that is the holistic feature the field tests.

activities.anchor: the 1947 AAA statement
activities.caption: order the relativism argument
activities.name: anRelativismOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the field's mature position on relativism, first to last:
items: Suspend your own categories and reconstruct the practice's internal logic first
Judgement, if it follows, follows understanding
The discipline this enforced is visible in classic results — witchcraft as a system for explaining misfortune
Where relativism and human rights collide, the field debates it in public rather than defaulting to either
config.why: Relativism is methodological (interpret before you judge) more than moral (never judge). Anthropology helped write the Universal Declaration precisely because relativism had taught it what universal claims require to be credible.

activities.anchor: online communities without societies
activities.caption: drag between the two concepts
activities.name: anSocietyCompare

config.prompt: Two concepts that can come apart. Drag the divider.

before.label: society
before.text: A bounded, relatively self-sufficient population with ongoing social relations and institutions. It can contain hundreds of communities at once, and it does not need anyone to feel part of it.

after.label: community
after.text: The felt side: belonging, mutual identification, the 'we' that can be summoned. It can exist without a society — an online guild is the standard example — and tracking how the two come apart is modern anthropology's growth area.

config.why: The four fields each hold a different slice of both: cultural anthropology watches communities reproduce in interaction, archaeology reads them from settlement plans, biological anthropology traces the populations beneath them, and linguistic anthropology listens to how the 'we' is spoken into being.

activities.anchor:
a child
    raised across the border is fluent in the other culture
activities.caption: file each feature of the core concept
activities.name: anCultureFeatureBuckets

config.prompt: Tylor's definition unpacks into features the field tests. File each example by the feature it demonstrates:

items.label: a child raised across the border becomes fluent in the other culture
language as the master case of meaning-laden signs
religion, economy, kinship and ecology interlocking

config.why: Everyone has culture, including financiers, engineers and readers of this page — the 'exotic others' framing is the discipline's oldest bad habit and its modern target.
